title: How Diamonds Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore diamonds: the 1982 Atlantic article by Ever J. Epstein about resale value and an experiment that found diamonds lose value when resold, the De Beers cartel and its marketing ("A diamond is forever"), how diamonds form deep in the mantle and reach the surface through kimberlite pipes, where diamonds are found (including alluvial deposits and cratons), how rough diamonds are cleaved, sawed, bruted, cut and polished, the Mohs hardness scale, the four Cs (cut, clarity, carat, color), conflict/blood diamonds and the Kimberley Process, synthetic and simulant stones (cubic zirconia, moissanite, lab-grown diamonds), and the Hope Diamond curse. The episode closes with a listener mail story about pickpockets in Madrid.

segments.title: Opening banter and diamond resale experiment
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter and introduce diamonds as a topic. Josh describes a 1982 Atlantic article by Ever J. Epstein in which a writer for Money bought a diamond, found its resale value was far below cost, and repeated the test with similar results.

segments.title: What diamonds are made of and where they form
segments.summary: Diamonds are made of carbon, which occurs as graphite, diamond and fullerite. Diamonds form deep in the mantle under high temperature and pressure, and eruptions pushed them up through kimberlite pipes.

segments.title: Where diamonds are found
segments.summary: Diamonds are found in kimberlite and in alluvial deposits moved by glaciers and water. Major sources include Russia, Borneo, Australia, Canada, Brazil, Venezuela and Africa, often in ancient cratons.

segments.title: Cleaving, sawing, bruting, cutting and polishing
segments.summary: Rough diamonds are cleaved along the tetrahedral plane of weakness or sawed with phosphor bronze blades. They are shaped by bruting or machine cutting on a lathe, then polished with diamond powder. Major cutting centers include New York, Bombay, Israel, Antwerp and Johannesburg.

segments.title: Mohs hardness scale and the four Cs
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Mohs hardness scale, which ranks diamond at the top, and then the four Cs used to value diamonds: cut, clarity, carat and color, along with brilliance and fire.

segments.title: Colored diamonds
segments.summary: Colored diamonds such as yellow, pink, green and black are rarer and more valuable than transparent diamonds.

segments.title: De Beers cartel and diamond marketing
segments.summary: De Beers, a cartel founded under Cecil Rhodes, controlled much of the diamond supply and sales through sights. Its marketing, including the 'Diamond is Forever' slogan, made diamonds a symbol of engagement and discouraged resale. Monopoly weakened around 2000 when Russia, Canada and Australia sold outside De Beers.

segments.title: Blood diamonds and the Kimberley Process
segments.summary: Conflict or blood diamonds fund rebel groups. The Kimberley Process certification scheme tries to track diamonds through government import and export certification, but critics say it does not cover cutting or polishing and ignores abuses by some governments. US executive orders and the Clean Diamond Trade Act addressed the issue.

segments.title: Synthetic diamonds and simulants
segments.summary: Cubic zirconia, moissanite and lab-grown diamonds are discussed. Cubic zirconia is a lab-made simulant, moissanite is silicon carbide, and lab-grown diamonds are structurally real diamonds, sold at a fraction of natural prices. Jewelers now use machines to detect them, made by De Beers.

segments.title: The Hope Diamond curse
segments.summary: The hosts recount the Hope Diamond's reputed curse, linking it to Tavernier, Louis XIV, George IV, Mademoiselle Lalaurie-type stories, the Sultan Abdul Hamid II, and Harry Winston's donation to the Smithsonian delivered by regular mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: pickpockets in Madrid
segments.summary: Liz writes about a school trip to Europe where a pickpocket tried to steal from a teacher in Madrid, and a Swedish rugby team caught him and recovered wallets.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener, invite feedback on social media and email, and promote the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
